idiom_name: func testUser(t testing.TB) User plus field assignment in the test
implementation_notes: Go has no default arguments and no builder classes in the standard toolkit: the idiomatic realization is a test helper in the package's _test.go file that returns a fully valid value (func testUser(t testing.TB) User { return User{Name: "Ada Lovelace", Email: "ada@example.com", Age: 30} }) and a test that overrides the single field it asserts on by assignment. Meaningful zero values and struct literals make plain fields the natural extension point, and t.Helper() keeps failure lines pointing at the test. A chainable builder struct reads un-idiomatically here; keep the helper-and-assign form unless callers must configure the value in one expression, where functional options are the local alternative.
pitfalls: Helpers that return pointers hand every test a shared instance; return values (or deep copies) so one test's assignment cannot leak into another.
Slice and map fields are reference values: overriding one in a test mutates the default unless the helper allocates a fresh collection per call.
The helper must be unexported and live in _test.go (or an internal test-support package), or it silently becomes part of the package's production API.

variants.name: Functional options for test data
variants.implementation_notes: Where tests want the override inline, Go's functional-options idiom carries the pattern: option functions of type func(*User) apply only the fields a caller passes (WithEmail("bad@example.com")), and a helper testUser(t, opts ...Option) starts from the same valid defaults, so the call site names exactly the variation. It costs one option constructor per field and one layer of indirection, and pays off when a factory must serve many differently shaped tests in a single expression or when the options are shared across packages.
pitfalls: Option functions mutate the value they are handed, so a base value reused across calls carries earlier options' effects; construct a fresh value per call.
One constructor per field is boilerplate that grows with the domain type and drifts when fields are added, so options are worth it only where the single-expression call site matters.
